title: Asking Nicely
summary: REST, GraphQL and gRPC — how the shape of an API decides round trips, bytes and safe retries on a flaky phone network.

goals.text: Describe resources and verbs in a REST API
Explain why round trips hurt most on mobile
Choose between a screen API, GraphQL and gRPC
Make retries safe with idempotency keys

steps.title: Things with addresses
body: Trailmix is a hiking app: trails, reviews, weather at the trailhead. Its first backend speaks REST: every thing (a trail, a user, a review) is a resource with a URL, and plain HTTP verbs say what to do with it.
Because the rules are shared by the whole web, a REST API is easy to explore with a browser, easy to cache (a GET is safe to store) and every language already has a client.

card.title: REST in one card
lines: # nouns live in the URL, verbs come from HTTP

steps.title: A truck to deliver a postcard
body: The new Nearby screen lists 20 trails with a name, distance and star rating. The only endpoint available is GET /trails, which returns each trail in full — GPS track, elevation profile, photo list.
That is over-fetching: the server sends 1.6 MB so the phone can draw 8 KB worth of text. On a metered data plan the user pays for it, and the screen waits for every byte.

callout.text: Adding ?fields=name,km helps, but every new screen then needs its own field list.

card.title: One list screen
lines: ! GPS tracks and photo lists ride along unused

steps.title: Four questions, one screen
body: The trail detail screen needs the trail, its author, the latest reviews and a forecast. With one endpoint per resource, the app has to call four of them — under-fetching.
Worse, the calls depend on each other: the app only learns the author's id and the trailhead coordinates from the first reply, so the requests run one after another in a waterfall.

steps.title: Latency beats bandwidth
body: On a phone, the cost of a request is mostly the round trip: radio wake-up, the signal travelling to a tower and on to the data center and back. A weak 3G link can add 300–400 ms per trip before a single byte of data arrives.
Four sequential round trips cost four times that wait. Shaving bytes barely matters; removing trips does.

callout.text: Design mobile APIs around one round trip per screen. Data-center hops between your own services cost ~1 ms; the phone's hop costs hundreds.

card.title: Time spent waiting
lines: # bytes are small; the round trips dominate

steps.title: Let the server do the running around
body: A backend for frontend (BFF) is a thin API shaped like the app's screens. The phone makes one call; the BFF fans out to Trails, Users, Reviews and Weather inside the data center, where each hop takes a millisecond or two, and returns exactly what the screen draws.
The cost: every new screen means BFF work, and a web app and a phone app often end up with a BFF each.
changes: + Screen API (BFF) in front of the services

steps.title: The client writes the order
body: GraphQL turns the BFF idea into a general tool. The server publishes a typed schema of everything it knows; the client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants, through one endpoint. Resolvers on the server fetch each piece.
No over-fetching, no under-fetching, and front-end teams can change a screen without waiting for a new endpoint.

callout.text: The bill comes later: one POST endpoint defeats ordinary HTTP caching, naive resolvers cause N+1 queries (batch them), and a hostile query can be enormous — enforce depth and cost limits.

card.title: The app asks for a shape

steps.title: Calling a function on another machine
body: Between your own services, a remote procedure call style often fits better than resources. With gRPC you describe functions and messages in a .proto file; tools generate typed client and server code, and calls travel as compact binary over HTTP/2.
You get strict contracts, smaller payloads, multiplexed connections, deadlines and streaming. Browsers can't speak it natively, so it usually lives behind the BFF or GraphQL layer.
changes: ~ Internal calls now gRPC over HTTP/2

steps.title: Old apps never die
body: Web pages update on refresh; installed apps don't. A year from now some hikers will still run v1, which reads distance in miles. If you rename it to distanceKm, their app breaks on the trail.

So APIs evolve additively: add new fields, keep old ones until usage drops, and reserve a new version (/v2 or a header) for changes that truly can't be additive. GraphQL marks fields @deprecated; protobuf never reuses a field number.
changes: + Old app v1 still in the wild

card.title: Change without breaking
lines: ! rename or remove a field: old apps crash
# big breaks: /v2/… path or a version header

steps.title: Did it work? Try again!
body: A hiker books a campsite as the train enters a tunnel. The server books it and charges the card, but the reply never reaches the phone. The app times out and does the reasonable thing: it retries.
POST is not idempotent: doing it twice does the thing twice. Networks lose replies all the time, so any API that clients retry must handle this.
changes: ~ The retry creates a second booking

card.title: A tunnel, a retry
lines: 3. app times out, sends POST again

steps.title: Same key, same answer
body: The app generates an idempotency key once per user action and sends it with every attempt. The server records each key with its result; a repeat with a known key gets the stored reply instead of a new booking.
Now the client may retry freely — on timeouts, on app restarts, even days later within the key's lifetime.

callout.text: Store the key and the booking in the same transaction, or a crash between the two reopens the gap.

card.title: Idempotency key
lines: new key → book, store the reply
same key again → return stored reply
= retry as often as you like
# GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent by design

steps.title: Pick the style per hop
body:
StyleBest at
RESTpublic APIs, cacheable reads, simple CRUD
Screen API / GraphQLphone and web clients — one trip per screen
gRPCservice-to-service: typed, binary, streaming

• Over-fetching wastes bytes; under-fetching wastes round trips — on mobile the trips hurt more.
  • Evolve APIs additively; old clients live for years.
  • Anything a client may retry needs an idempotency story.
